content.title: About
content.content: Farm‑raised shrimp are a seafood product obtained in controlled aquaculture systems. Raw farm shrimp have a delicate, slightly sweet flavor and a firm yet tender texture. They are suitable for salads, sushi, quick marinades and dishes that require brief cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Farmed shrimp are raised in closed‑loop tanks where temperature, salinity and feed are tightly regulated.
Compared with wild shrimp, farmed ones usually have a more uniform size and color.
Shrimp belong to the crustacean class, making them close relatives of crayfish and lobsters.
The majority of global shrimp production comes from Asian countries such as China, Thailand and Vietnam.
Raw shrimp are often sold frozen in sealed bags, which preserves freshness and nutrients.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Shrimp provide about 20 g of high‑quality animal protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Less than 1 g of fat per 100 g, yet they contain beneficial omega‑3 fatty acids.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for red blood cell formation and nervous system health; shrimp supply a substantial amount.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Shrimp deliver selenium, zinc, iron and iodine, which aid immune function and thyroid health.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Astaxanthin and lutein in shrimp help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Shrimp are a common allergen; reactions can be severe.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw shrimp may harbor salmonella or vibrio; proper hygiene and cooking to safe temperatures are essential.

items.title: High cholesterol content
items.content: Approximately 150 mg of cholesterol per 100 g; individuals with hypercholesterolemia should monitor intake.

items.title: Purines
items.content: Shrimp are rich in purines, which can exacerbate gout in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Thaw frozen shrimp in the refrigerator, then quickly sauté, boil, or steam for 2–3 minutes. Add them to salads, rice dishes, pasta, sushi, or use in marinades. A squeeze of lemon or a dash of soy sauce is a common finishing touch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen shrimp in an airtight bag at –18 °C. Once thawed, use within 1–2 days and store in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C. Do not leave at room temperature for more than 2 hours to prevent bacterial growth.
